lines.text: Both engines just quit on the plane Gus is on, seven miles up, and the only thing that stops is his movie.
It's three in the afternoon, and Gus is halfway through a movie.
Then it all goes quiet and the screen goes black. His neighbor grabs his seat.
We'll drop like a rock, yells Gus, but his wife just eats her sandwich.
But wait. The plane isn't dropping. Why not?
You see, the engines never held the plane up. The wings do that, and engines only push.
Ever coast down a hill on a bike? You stop pedaling, and you keep rolling.
A plane does the same. It rolls down a hill made of air.
And that hill is not steep. For each mile it sinks the plane slides fifteen miles ahead.
That's flatter than a wheelchair ramp.
So from seven miles up it glides over a hundred miles, for almost twenty minutes.
A jet once ran out of fuel and glided seventy-five miles to an island, and they all lived.
Luckily, a little propeller drops from the belly and spins in the wind to power the controls.
Unluckily, it's too small to run the movie screens.
And here's the thing. On a normal flight the pilots pull the engines back to idle a hundred miles out.
Gus has been gliding home his whole life. He just never knew it till the movie stopped.
